paper.title: Accelerating the Discovery of Hybrid Perovskites with Targeted Band Gaps via Interpretable Machine Learning
paper.file_name: 36_Accelerating the Discovery of Hybrid Perovskites with Targeted Band Gaps via Interpretable Machine Learning.pdf
paper.research_summary: This study combined feature engineering, the gradient-boosted regression tree (GBRT) algorithm, and the genetic algorithm-based symbolic regression (GASR) algorithm to develop an interpretable machine learning (ML) strategy for predicting the band gap of hybrid organic−inorganic perovskites (HOIPs) accurately and quantitatively interpreting the factors affecting the band gap. Seven best physical features were selected to construct a GBRT model with a root-mean-square error of less than 0.060 eV, and the most important feature is the electronegativity difference between the B-site and the X-site (χB−X). Further, a mathematical formula (Eg = χB−X^2 + 0.881χB−X) was constructed with GASR for a quantitative interpretation of the band gap influence patterns. According to the ML model, the HOIP MA0.23FA0.02Cs0.75Pb0.59Sn0.41Br0.24I2.76 was obtained, with a suitable band gap of 1.39 eV.

tasks.task_name_raw: predicting the experimental band gap values of HOIPs
tasks.objective: to predict the experimental band gap values of hybrid organic−inorganic perovskites (HOIPs) using an interpretable ML strategy
material_scope: ABX3 (A = Cs, formamidinium (FA), or methylammonium (MA); B = Pb or Sn; X = Br, Cl, or I)
input_requirements: physical features (e.g., electronegativity, ionic radius, Goldschmidt tolerance factor, octahedral factor, electron affinity, dipole polarizability, atomic radius, d/f orbital electrons)
output_goal: HOIP compositions with targeted band gaps (e.g., MA0.23FA0.02Cs0.75Pb0.59Sn0.41Br0.24I2.76 with 1.39 eV)

evidence.text: the focus of this work is to predict the experimental band gap values of HOIPs using an interpretable ML strategy.

stages.stage_goal: to ensure the quantity and accuracy of the data
stage_output: data set consisting of HOIPs’ experimental band gaps

evidence.text: Data Preparation. To ensure the quantity and accuracy of the data, two principles were used in the data collection and cleaning process. First, we selected compounds with a three-dimensional structure of ABX3 (A-site = Cs, FA, or MA; B-site = Pb or Sn; X-site = Br, Cl, or I). Second, for data with the same composition but different band gaps, we chose the average value when the difference between the maximum value and the minimum value is less than 0.2 eV. When it is greater than 0.2 eV, we chose the model because the experimental error is about 0.1−0.2 eV when using different instruments. All data points were collated from the PSC database built by Jacobsson et al.16 Eventually, the total data set consists of 610 data points with known band gap values.

stage_input: data set consisting of HOIPs’ experimental band gaps

evidence.text: Then, we randomly divided 15% of the data set as the test set to evaluate the generalization capability for all ML models, and the remaining 85% as the training set to train all ML models.

stages.stage_goal: to replace simple atomic ratio features with physical features to facilitate physical interpretations
stage_input: initial feature pool based on a priori knowledge (Pauling’s electronegativity, μ, τ, IR, EA, DP, AR, d/f orbital electrons)
stage_output: 11 groups of highly correlated descriptors and the retained ones

evidence.text: In order to validate the accuracy of the data set and comparison with the subsequent model with physical features as input, we simultaneously trained models with composition (ML-C) as features using multiple algorithms... To further enhance the physical interpretability, we used physical features to replace the simple atomic ratio features as the model inputs (ML-P). Previous works have shown that the excellent model’s performance can be obtained by employing electronic properties-related and structure-related features such as electronegativity, Goldschmidt tolerance factor (τ), and octahedral factor (μ). In this work, we chose nine element characteristics as descriptors in the initial feature pool based on a priori knowledge...

stages.stage_goal: to construct a high-performance prediction model and explain the importance of the feature

evidence.text: Next, the GBRT algorithm was used to construct a high-performance prediction model and explain the importance of the feature.

Figure 3b shows the variation of GBRT-P accuracy with the number of subfeatures; the model accuracy is not significantly improved when the number of subfeatures is greater than 7, so we chose the top 7 features in ranked feature importance as input variables to reduce the complexity of the model without sacrificing the accuracy too much and the final GBRT-P model with an RMSE of 0.059 eV for the test set.

stages.stage_goal: to assess model performance using RMSE and R²

evidence.text: Among them, the GBRT-P model has the best performance with the RMSE and R2 values of the test set equal to 0.059 and 0.99, respectively (Figure 2a).

stages.stage_goal: to obtain mathematical formulas that quantify the relationships between features and predictive properties

evidence.text: Finally, using the GASR algorithm allowed clear mathematical formulations to be obtained for quantitative analysis of the band gaps.
To explicitly obtain the mapping between physical features and the band gap, we used the GASR algorithm to develop mathematical formulas between 7 features and band gaps.

After trading off the complexity and accuracy of the formula, we chose the formula Eg = χB−X^2 + 0.881χB−X as the best formula with the highest accuracy, RMSE = 0.84 eV for the test set, and the lowest complexity was 3.

stages.stage_goal: to identify HOIP compositions with targeted band gaps (1.3−1.4 eV and 1.7−2.1 eV)
stage_output: compositions not in original data set with band gaps in target ranges

evidence.text: In this work, GBRT-P was used for band gap prediction for composition screening, which has both high accuracy and interpretability. We focused on the ideal band gap range (1.3−1.4 eV) and wide band gap range (1.7−2.1 eV) to find potential compositions.

stages.stage_goal: to select compositions for experimental synthesis
stage_input: compositions not in original data set with band gaps in target ranges

evidence.text: Finally, we randomly selected three groups among the remaining compositions for the experimental synthesis.

stages.stage_goal: to validate predictions by measuring band gaps of synthesized HOIPs

evidence.text: Three compositions were experimentally synthesized, and the XRD results are presented in Figure 4b, indicating that all three compositions possess pure perovskite structures. The band gap values, measured by UV−vis spectra, are shown in Figure 4c.

evidence.text: Figure 4a shows the distribution of the selected experimental validation compositions in the feature space of the training set and test set; it can be seen that they are far away from the known composition in the feature space, and none of the three compositions have been published in the public literature at present.

Three compositions were experimentally synthesized, and the XRD results are presented in Figure 4b, indicating that all three compositions possess pure perovskite structures. The band gap values, measured by UV−vis spectra, are shown in Figure 4c.
